utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. We are noticing that we're slipping further behind schedule. I think that it is important that we become aware of that. There are a large number of witnesses in this trial. The evidence of many of them is really of relevance only to one or two issues, and there needs to be a sharper focus by counsel on the relevance of the witness and less attention to minor detail in examination and cross-examination if we are to complete the hearing of this case in a reasonable time. For instance, this week a witness we might have reached today will clearly not be reached until Monday, and there are two earlier witnesses yet to be heard. I would encourage counsel, both for the Prosecution and the Defence, to be extremely mindful of time as we go through the two witnesses for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation that's shown to you now on the card.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. Ms. Kravetz has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: My name is Sabit Kadriu.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, did you provide a statement to the Office of the Prosecution in 2000?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to read your statement before coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In proofing you made two corrections to your statement. I am going to read out each of those corrections and ask you to confirm if the correction has been clearly stated. In page 6, paragraph 4, third sentence, currently reads: "I must mention here that after the war I cooperated with the LDK, but as a result developed some differences with the council ..." Did you correct this sentence to simply read: "I must mention here that after the war I cooperated with the LDK ..." and indicated that the rest of this sentence should be deleted as that information is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Page 9 contains a list of the victims of the massacre of the village in Galice at the top of the page. Did you indicate that two names had been omitted from this list and should have been included in your statements. And these are the names of Sejdi Kabashi, 24 years old of the village of Polac; and Enver Kabashi, 36 years old of the village of Poluza?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Other than for those two corrections, are you satisfied that the information contained in your statement is true and accurate to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I seek to tender this statement into evidence, Your Honour, this is 65 ter 02377.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00515, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, did you also testify previously before this Tribunal in the case of Milutinovic et al.?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Before coming to court today, did you have the opportunity to go over the transcript of your previous testimony with the assistance of a language assistant?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In proofing you indicated that you wanted to clarify one -- one information that's contained in paragraph -- in transcript page 5.073, line 16, of the Milutinovic transcript and this is page 18 in e-court. This line currently reads: "Simic was deputy police commander, Dusko Janjic --" You indicated that this should actually state: "Simic was deputy police commander of Vucina Janivecic?" Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Simic was deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Other than for that clarification, if you were asked the same questions that you were asked in your previous testimony, would you provide the same answers today?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this transcript. This is 65 ter 05093.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00516, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, in order to proceed efficiently with the exhibits associated to this transcript, I would propose to read each one of the 65 ter numbers out so the Registrar can assign an exhibit number if that pleases Your Honours. I will proceed in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: These are the exhibits are listed in the annex B to our 92 bis motion. First Exhibit is 65 ter 00008, and I seek to tender that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00517, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Second exhibit is 00046, and I ask that that be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00518, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Next one is 00053, and I ask that that exhibit be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00519, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Next exhibit is 02386, and I ask that that be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00520, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Next exhibit is 01335, and I ask that that be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00521, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The next one is 00477, and I seek to tender that exhibit as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00522, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Next exhibit 01334, and I ask that that be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00523, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Next exhibit 00487, and I ask that that be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00524, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And the last exhibit is 02393, and I ask that that be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00525, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Witness, the Chamber has your previous testimony and your statement -- written statement already before them. I have very few questions for you, and I'm going to direct your attention to page 21 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: For this purpose I ask that the witness be provided a hard copy just for ease of reference. It's page 20 in the Albanian version.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, in your statement you described events that took place in the municipality of Vucitrn on 2nd May, specifically on that page you have listed over 100 victims that died in a convoy massacre that took place on 2nd of May. I would like you to explain for Your Honours how you collected the names which are listed in your statement starting on page 21 up to page 24 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: It was not a problem for me to collect the names because I too was a member in that convoy on the 2nd of May, but the fact is that on the night that the monstrous crime was committed when about 100 persons were killed, I didn't know the exact number of the dead. But after I was released from prison and with the entry of the NATO forces in Kosova, the conditions were created for us to conduct an investigation into the event because that night I could not be in a position to know that such number was the case. I heard only that 60 persons were killed from a conversation among the policemen, but after the war we realised that over 100 persons were executed in a very short time. That's why I worked on the case. I started investigating family by family together with the members of the commission where I was a member of. It was a commission on the investigation of the Serb crimes, after the war, that I chaired. Being a member of that convoy, I felt it my obligation to go through to the end of this case. And in this place there is a monument erected now and there are all the graves of the persons executed in the night of the 2nd of May. They are well taken care of graves. There is a monument at the entrance to the cemetery in memory of the dead killed on the 2nd of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, you referred to conducting an investigation into this event. When you were conducting this investigation, did you interview witnesses of the convoy, persons who had been present when these killings occurred?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We organised ourselves as a group of this commission, and we went to take evidence for every single case from the family members of the persons killed that night, those family members that managed to return after the war from Albania and Montenegro to Kosova. We created a special file, drawing up a sketch of the route followed by the convoy from Sllakovc, Studime e Eperme, until Studime e Poshteme, and up to Vushtrri, which was the final destination. We handed over this evidence which shows in details the movement of the convoy on the 2nd of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You referred to preparing or creating a special file. Did you have the opportunity to consult that file when you provided this list that is contained in your statement to our investigators?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course. We had to be very careful in drawing up the list because even if one single person was not included in the list, it would show a failure in our work. That's why we did our best, we had a lot of time to work on the case until we came up with that list. Even though we had a lot of difficulties in our work, after the war, we didn't have all the necessary equipment, but we did manage to prepare the file and to interview the members of the families of the dead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You told us earlier that you yourself were a member of this convoy. I would like you to look at the list and tell me if you recognise any of the names as persons you knew and whom you saw that evening in the convoy.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes. I know many of them. Some of them I knew only by sight, but there are some whom I know by name and last name because, as you know, often it happens that you know someone by sight, you don't know the name and last name, and often you have them as acquaintances. From Gerxhaliu family, I know Kadri Gerxhaliu, with his brother who was present and was executed there; then I know Shaban Gerxhaliu. I used to know some others, Musa Abazi a professor, with who I worked in the high school in Vushtrri; and other names I know whom I saw that eventful night before the crime was committed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You said you knew Kadri Gerxhaliu and his brother. Do you recall Kadri Gerxhaliu's brother's name?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, for the moment I can't recall his name. He was a student of medicine. He was executed together with his brother. Then it was Shaban Kadriu's uncle who was also executed with his son. Then there was Enver Prronaj whom I used to know because of some family links. I saw him together with his family before the crime was committed. He was killed with his brother, whose name I don't know, whereas his name I know, that is Enver Prronaj. And some of them I met, with some of them I talked before the crime on the way because they were driving their tractors. I was alone walking, and I could walk slowly but I could meet a lot of people along the convoy. Since I was alone, I didn't have a family with me, I didn't have to drive a tractor or a cart, so I greeted people. I saw also some others whose names I didn't know but whose faces were familiar, like Skender Haki Gerxhaliu and others. There are several names actually that are here which I used to know. There are some whom, as I said, I knew only by sight but whose names I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, you have the list before you. I would ask you if you could have a look and just indicate if there are persons who are on this list that you have prepared who you recall seeing on the convoy before the massacre took place. You have already given us the names of some of the members of the Gerxhaliu --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Musa Abazi, for example, I knew him very well. I worked with Musa. We were colleagues in the high school -- in the higher -- correction, high school in Vushtrri.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did you have --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Then, as I said, I knew Skender Gerxhaliu from the Gerxhaliu family. Kadri Gerxhaliu, Shaban Gerxhaliu, Haki Gerxhaliu also was the brother of Skender. I used to know Bajram Muliqi. I knew the Prronaj family, Enver Prronaj and his family. I don't know the name of his other family members, with the exception of his wife who was my sister's sister-in-law. My sister was married to that family she came from, so I knew her in-laws. I saw them in their -- with their tractor. These are some names that I recall. There are many others that I, as I said, knew by sight whose names I didn't know. We simply greeted each other when we saw each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And if -- just to be clear on your answer, these names that you have mentioned today are all persons that you personally saw in the convoy when you were travelling with the convoy on 2 May?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, not only them, as I said, but I saw thousands of other people. But these were in the convoy together with their families on their tractors with their women, children; and as I said I stopped by and talked with them, especially those that I knew better. I met others as well, but these are the ones that I remember now since I had some family links with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to move away from that incident, as it's covered extensively in your written statement, and I just want to ask you a few questions in relation to a separate incident that is referred to in your statement. This is in paragraph -- on page 24 of your statement you refer to a killing that took place on 22nd May, 1999, and you also provide a list of victims to that incident. Is this an incident that you also investigated yourself?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, this is also an incident that I investigated together with the members of the committee of the investigation of crimes committed by the Serbs in Kosova. And allow me on this occasion -- if you allow me, your distinguished Prosecutor, to ask the honourable Court that on the 22nd of May very early in the morning after a large part of the city of Vushtrri was encircled west -- east of the city the army forces came, the police forces came from the western part along with voluntaries and other groups that had come from Serbia, groups of paramilitaries and police groups who evicted the family members from their homes. And on the 22nd of May they were directing them towards the cemetery of the city, separating some of the family members from the convoy because they had to pass through a cordon of policemen. These policemen and paramilitaries who had also their armoured vehicles and most of them were wearing masks or Balaclavas, they separated, as I said, some of them and asked them to enter the house of Sezai Pasoma and some other houses. After they entered this house, they executed 74 persons within a very short time. At this time, the process of rallying the people near the cemetery continued and houses continued to be burned and set on fire. So on this road, which is now called 22nd of May, 74 persons were killed. When I came here to testify in the Milosevic trial, these persons were described as missing persons, but the fact is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I simply wanted to make an explanation because I feel morally responsible towards their families because most of those executed on the 22nd of May returned but there are some who are still missing. And I think that this is an opportune moment to carry out the behest of their families which kindly asked me to ask this honourable Court to know about the destiny -- something about the destiny of those other missing persons. When they were executed on the 22nd of May --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there, Mr. Kadriu. Do you have information of -- on the fate of the victims that were killed on the 22nd of May?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes. This is where I wanted to come to. The fate of these victims was a tragic ones. They were all executed, the 74 of them. After that they were loaded into trucks and probably transported to the mass grave of Batajnica, which is 300 kilometres away from our town. Batajnica is a shooting ground for the Serb special forces, and the accused who is present here in the court is more than anyone responsible for such persons --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: -- he should tell us how it came that these 74 persons were transported from Vushtrri and taken to such a military base for the special forces in Belgrade. I apologise, but I wanted to say this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: How do you know that these persons -- the bodies of these persons were found at Batajnica?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I know because after 2002 representatives from this Tribunal exhumed dead bodies from this mass grave in Batajnica and the corpses of most of them, 70 per cent of the corpses, were returned to their families, the remains of their bodies. So I was present in all the burials of such persons whose fate ended in such a tragical manner in the mass grave of Batajnica in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kadriu.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness in relation to his evidence. I do realise I forgot to read out the court summary for this witness. I'm going to proceed to do that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The witness -- I'm going to proceed to read a court summary of your evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't get translation. Now, yes, I get it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The witness was the President of the Council for Human Rights in Vucitrn municipality. He describes the situation in his municipality during the Serb offensive in the summer of 1998 and the build-up of Serb forces at the end of February --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel is kindly asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: -- at the end of February 1999. On 27th March, 1999, the witness observed Serb forces setting fire to private homes and destroying a mosque in the centre of Vucitrn town. As a result of the attacks across Vucitrn municipality, the civilian population was displaced to the south-west of the municipality. The witness speaks about the convoy massacre that took place on the Gornja Sudimlja road on 2nd May, 1999. He was one of the refugees on the convoy. He describes that Serb forces attacked the convoy, and he provides the names of the victims. After the massacre, Serb forces ordered the surviving refugees to proceed in the direction of Vucitrn town. Serb forces led a group of more than 1.000 refugees through Donja Sudimlja to an agricultural co-operative outside Vucitrn. The refugees remained at the compound overnight. On 3rd May, 1999, Serb police separated Kosovo Albanian men from women, children, and elderly, loaded them onto trucks and drove them to Smrekovnica prison in Vucitrn municipality. The witness was among the men who were imprisoned at this prison. He describes the inhumane conditions of detention. On 23rd of May, 1999, the detainees were released and had all their identification documents taken from them prior to crossing the border at Zhur into Albania. That's the end of the court summary of this witness's evidence, and that's also the end of my questioning at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Kravetz. Mr. Kadriu, I think we should explain to you a little of the procedure we're following because it's very clear that you want to give a long explanation of a number of things that have impressed themselves very deeply on you. You may understand that we have received this morning, tendered through you, the full statement you made back in the year 2000 and a full transcript of the evidence that you've already given in this Tribunal in the Milutinovic trial. The Chamber has all of that material and the things that you are wanting to say now from my assessment of it are things you have also said earlier, both in your statement and particularly in the evidence you gave in Milutinovic. It's to avoid unnecessarily repeating all that that we are using the statement and the transcript. So we have before us already the things that you are wanting to say again. Don't think they're being ignored or overlooked. We have them. What now happens is that the Defence in this case will be questioning you in case there are issues important in this case that haven't been considered in the earlier evidence that you gave or may need to be highlighted from your statement. And we then take all of that into account. I thought I should explain that to you so you understand. Thank you. Now, Mr. Djordjevic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before the counsel begins with his questions, it is true what you just said, I did give a statement, but things have changed since then. The truth is when, I testified in the Milosevic trial, we didn't know anything about the fate of 74 persons. So as the time went by, light was shed on many things. So as the years went by, we were able to see what actually happened in our town, this terrible crime. So please don't misunderstand me when I put forward some requests before you on behalf of family members. In Prishtina a few days ago, there was a protest organised by family members of the missing persons because there are about 1.784 persons unaccounted for. So this is the best medium for me to put forward this request to find out about the fate of these missing persons. The family members of these missing persons, when I go back in Kosova, will probably ask me about their dear ones. So that's why I thought this was the best place to put forward this request, for the accused to tell us where the mass graves are so that these families find out where the remains of their dearest ones are. And that would make the job easier even for this Trial Chamber, because that would enable the Trial Chamber to understand better what had happened in Kosova in 1998 and 1999. I think it would have been even easier for the accused, it would be a relief for him to tell us where the mass graves containing the remains of our parents, of our brothers and sisters, are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please understand we are hearing not only you, we are hearing a number of other witnesses concerning the important events, and we are hearing a lot of evidence about those bodies that have been found, the remains of people, and of bodies that have not yet been found. So it's not just you on this day. This trial is going to take a year or so to complete. We will have over 120 Prosecution witnesses. So understand we're putting together a great deal of information of what is known today; and from that we must then reach our conclusions. So please, don't think that you are not being heard or that the concerns of those you are advancing to us are being ignored. We are well conscious of them, but you will understand because there is so much evidence we need to hear it as quickly as we can and to move efficiently through the body so that we can get the full picture, and that's what we're trying to do today, so thank you. Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Kadriu.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, I will take very little time, but I would like to ask the witness and to say something that the Defence shouldn't really be doing but since it is on the record, the witness has asked about things that he knows, about facts, not about what he thinks, and the witness cannot violate the presumption of innocence and cannot urge the accused to tell the families where all the mass graves are located. And since this is a prominent intellectual from Kosovo who headed the Human Rights Council according to the CV that we received, I would like to ask the witness to comply with the sacred legal principles that we all have to abide by, but let me move on to my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, I will be asking you only about things that I deem to be relevant for this case, not only for the Defence --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I didn't prejudice anyone. I only stated what is a fact, that this figure I gave you is the exact figure of the people missing. I'm a competent witness, and I competently state that this accused was responsible for the transportation of bodies and their burial in this mass grave --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I must stop you. You've been allowed a great deal of liberty to speak without questions. We need to proceed efficiently, and we need to deal with the evidence. If you would please listen to the questions and answer those, and that will enable us to reach as reliable a conclusion as we can at the end of the trial. Thank you very much. And you, Mr. Djordjevic, will appreciate that this Chamber has regard to the onus of proof and it is for us and not a witness to be considering that. So if you could move into your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, now I would like to you to tell us, you headed the Human Rights Council as the chairman. Could you please tell me, where was the seat of the Human Rights Council?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: That is true. I headed the Human Rights Council in Vushtrri. I was the chairman of this council's branch in Vushtrri. There was a hierarchy. The main office was in Pristina and every town had the local branchs. I was the chairman of the Human Rights Council for the territory of Vushtrri.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kadriu. Would you please tell me, as the chairman of the council for the Vucitrn area, what were the objectives, the goals, of what I assume to be an NGO, a non-governmental organisation?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: It is true that the council was an NGO. The Human Rights Council was formed as a requirement of time with the -- once the autonomy of Kosova was revoked, the violation of the rights of ethnic Albanians from Kosova continued. That's why there was a need for this council to be established in the capital and in other towns. So our main duty was to investigate cases of violation of rights of citizens in the territory of Vushtrri municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me who founded the Human Rights Council in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: In the 1990s the Human Rights Council in Pristina, i.e., in Kosova, was created by a group of intellectuals headed by Idriz Ajeti, Pajazit Nushi, and Adem Demaqi, after he was released from prison, joined the Human Rights Council and subsequently was appointed chairman of the Human Rights Council. As you know, Adem Demaqi was sentenced to 28 years of prison because of his activities in protecting the rights of people in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next question is this: You told me that this council was founded because the autonomy of the citizens in Kosovo had been reduced. I take it that you're referring only to the citizens of Albanian ethnicity when you say that; am I right?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: That's correct. In 1989, the autonomy of the citizens in Kosova was reduced. The majority in Kosova were Albanians, 95 per cent; the remaining percentage, the Serbs, enjoyed all their rights, even greater rights than the citizens in democratic countries of Europe. However, the Albanians were stripped the right to education, our schools were no longer available to us, there was no employment for the Albanians, they were removed from their jobs in factories that they had founded, they were stripped of their right to social insurance and other benefits. So the autonomy of 1974 was revoked in this year. Even Albanian mothers were no longer entitled to give birth in hospitals. We couldn't even organise funeral cemeteries as they should be organised.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Funeral ceremonies, correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next question is this: Do you have any knowledge of violations of human rights of Serbs and other non-Albanians in Kosovo about any threats to their property, to their personal safety, violations of their personal integrity, crimes against honour of these people? Do you have any knowledge of that? Did you protect their rights too?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Of course we protected the rights of all the people who were suppressed by the government. If the government or the administration committed violation of human rights against any citizen, we investigated the case, of course, if the citizen was willing for us to carry out such an investigation. As the administration was a Serb administration, it doesn't make sense that that would violate the rights of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... as the chairman? As the chairman did you draft any reports containing any Serb names or Roma names or names of any other ethnicity, Turkish and so on? Did you make any reports that concerned human rights violations of non-Albanians?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: If a government regime, police organs, administration, indiscriminately violated the rights of citizen regardless of their ethnicity, we would investigate. A Serb person was killed, and he was taken to --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Answer my question. I have to interrupt you. You were warned by the Trial Chamber that our time is precious. Did you make a single report, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: You asked a question, and I think you should wait for me to complete my answer. I will give you my answer as I think I should answer your question not as you want me to. What I said is the following: If the government with its organs, with legislative system, police system, and the judiciary, violated the rights of any citizen, there were such cases, we would investigate; but, as I said, they did not violate the rights of the Serbs with the exception of one case when one Serb was killed. You're looking at me now as if I didn't give you an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is your answer to the question no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there were such cases, yes, we would compile reports; but the government was a Serb government and they didn't violate the rights of the Serbs. They served their best to these 5 or 6 per cent of the population that was Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djordjevic, continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you protected those rights if they were under threat, but were they under threat and did you draft a single report - let me ask you again - dealing with the human rights violations of non-Albanians, Serbs, Turks, and so on in Vucitrn, yes or no? So I can conclude that there were no violations of their human rights; am I right?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: There were such cases. I mentioned one case, and I do have other cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next question: As the chairman of the Human Rights Council, I assume that you are familiar with all the human rights conventions, am I right, international conventions that deal with human rights?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: You're right. The Geneva Convention, I read it all. I'm not a lawyer by profession; but due to the circumstances, I did read it carefully, the Geneva Conventions of 1949.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you understand that protection of human rights does not entail only violations that are carried out by governments, but that there are other forms of human rights violations?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: That's correct. But the nature of our work was such, that is to say to investigate cases of violence and repression carried by governmental organs, police, army, and so on. But what you said is correct, there were such cases too, and we did take them down -- noted them down.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's why I'm asking you. Apart from chronicling what you did, we know about it from the record and from your statement, did you also chronicle the destruction of Serb property, serious violations of human rights that occurred before 1998 and 1997 or not? Since you say that your organisation was established in the 1990s, if I'm not wrong.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Look, sir, who could have possibly committed destruction of Serb property when everything was in the hands of the Serbs? Who dared commit violation of the rights of Serbs when the Albanians were not even allowed to freely live in their own houses? There were no such cases. The Serb government did not allow us to live in peace in our own houses. Had they done that, had we been free to exercise our rights, there wouldn't have been a KLA, there wouldn't have been a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You say 95 per cent Albanians and 5 per cent Serbs. Where did you get those figures? Are you aware of some census that I'm not aware of?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I'm referring to the statistical data of the census carried out by the Yugoslav government in 1981. There was no census after this in Kosova. These should be the approximate figures with minor change I would say, 0 point something, but this was the structure of the population, respectable Counsel. We cannot change it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you for your answer, but there is -- there are official data from the last census in Kosovo, and according to those data the ratio is not 95:5 per cent, but at any rate the Albanian population was in the majority and that's why I asked you this question about the threats to the human rights of Serbs in Kosovo. But since you say that the Serbs' rights could not be jeopardised -- please --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Albanians were an absolute majority, but the government did not belong to us. We didn't have power. As a peoples, we were the majority, but it was the Serb government and the Yugoslav government that had the power after 1989. So 95 per cent were governed by 5 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What I want to know -- well, I'm not going to be asking you about the political goals of the KLA. I'm going to ask you about the political goals of the Albanians, or rather, those who were the intellectual elite of the nation in Kosovo. So could you please tell me what were the political goals of the Albanian intellectual elite? You spoke about that in your statement but I would like to ask you a direct question so that I can get an answer from you.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Counsel, can you be more precise. What period of time are you referring to so that I can give you a more concise answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm talking about the period that was the watershed, in your words, when the autonomy was -- when the Albanians, the citizens of Albanian ethnicity, were stripped of their autonomy and when the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and of the Republic of Serbia were amended in such a way that Kosovo was stripped of its autonomy, then there were demonstrations. I don't want to ask you about that, about who participated, whether they were students or not. But I want you to tell me what were the goals of the Albanians in light of the situation that existed at the time?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: To survive, to survive. After the revocation of Kosova's autonomy in 1989, our very survival was at stake. We were dismissed from work, from institutions, we were driven out of schools of children's creches; we were deprived of normal conditions to live. I think this was a genocidal act even though it is described as crime against humanity by the Tribunal based on the Geneva Convention, it turns out to be a genocide.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that later, but my question was, let me repeat, please listen carefully: What were the political goals of the Albanians? Would you please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The witness has answered that in a general way, but the question is extremely general and it is perhaps naive to suggest that all Albanians or all Albanian elite intellectuals had one political goal. Now, Mr. Djordjevic, we want you to appreciate that while there may be a very important and interesting discussion for a lot of reasons about the general political background and circumstances, this Chamber is concerned with some very specific events in 1999, not with the long history over the years that preceded that. And therefore, while we give you the liberty to ask some limited questions about the background, the attention needs to be focused on the matters dealt with the indictment. If you could keep that in mind and it would be useful if your questions were very specific rather than so general, that would assist then the answer to be specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that the goal of the Albanians was Kosovo Republic and that's -- that that was the basic demand?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: That's right. This was a request we had since 1981, yes, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And would it be correct that it was every Albanian's dream for all Albanians to live in a single state?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: We have this dream even today because we were unjustly separated in 1913. It's like having -- the people is like having a body. If you cut off the limbs of this body, you feel like you are handicapped, you are disabled, and our people was divided in two -- in five states, and this was an unjust act.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Is the reason for the founding of the Kosovo Liberation Army precisely to realise that dream and aim and the beginning of the armed conflict against the Serb forces in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: No. In 1981 there was no KLA. There were only students, youths, workers who wanted Kosova Republic. From 1981 onwards when the KLA was created, many years have passed --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I gave you the answer. It was the Yugoslav forces, the forces of Vlastimir Djordjevic, the police forces, and the forces of General Pavkovic that helped create the Kosova Liberation Army, it was due to this violence that people organised themselves into an army to defend themselves. I think if you were in the same situation you would have done the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Now, my next question is this: Since you were on the territory of Vucitrn, can you tell me in percentages how much of the territory was under the control of the KLA and how much under the control of the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, it's hard for me to speak in percentages because the KLA forces didn't have a permanent territory so to say. They had a part of territory for a while. They waged guerilla warfare, and as you know, you can't speak of permanent hold on territories. I cannot give you percentages. They held part of territory for a while, then they moved about, moved away from that and held another territory. They were, as I said, guerilla forces. They couldn't wage a frontal war because the Yugoslav power, might, was so strong that it routed them having so many planes, tanks, cannons, missiles, and so on. It was -- it is absurd to think that guerilla warfare can meet up to such a might. It's not that they didn't want to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about how frequently clashes occurred in the period let's say between March 1999 and June when the conflict ended with the bombing, the NATO bombing, and so on? How frequently were there clashes and conflicts between the KLA and Serb forces? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, there were clashes, that's a fact. But when the Serb forces used 80 armoured vehicles against Albanian ethnic villages, the KLA of course, waged an attack and then it withdrew to defend the villages, tried to cause some harm to this military machine of the army and the police. There were such clashes, yes, but there were clashes on both sides. What the army and the police left the barracks, of course they didn't go there to play football, your counsel, they went there to set fire to the houses, to kill people, to destroy everything they found there using the tactic of scorched land.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Bislim Zyrapi is?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I've heard about him, yes, I've heard about Bislim Zyrapi, but I don't know him. I never met him. I simply heard about him through newspaper articles, radio, television, but I don't know him at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether the KLA - and you said it conducted guerilla warfare - whether it used civilians frequently, Albanians?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: No, no, it didn't need to. It was absurd what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of anybody having issued an order, that is to say by the KLA commanders, that the population should withdraw from a given territory due to circumstances on the ground and the change of circumstances? Have you ever heard of anything like that?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, my next question is this: Do you know how the KLA was organised? Was it organised as an army or was it ad hoc organisation? Do you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes. I was not the general of that army. I dealt with human rights. But to give an answer to your question, I may say, as I said earlier, that the KLA had its guerilla units. It was not an organised army. Had it been such an army, I don't think the Serb forces could have penetrated the country and committed 50.000 killings and, Vlastimir Djordjevic couldn't have come to Kosova as many times as he wished. He has come from Kosova from north to south, but unfortunately we didn't have a powerful army. Had we had such an army, things would have been different.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Was Kosovo -- well, Kosovo and Metohija, the autonomous province, was it the territory of the sovereign state of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Republic of Serbia? And I don't see what's strange about any Serbian citizens going into the territory of their own country, their own state.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: It was, but it was annexed violently as a territory. You know that following the Second World War there was a movement against unification of Kosova with Albania. This happened immediately after the Second World War, and the government, the Yugoslav government of that time, committed a massacre, a massacre against the population of Drenice because they didn't want Kosova to remain under Yugoslavia. You know the time of Shaban Polluzha? He took part in the war against fascism. Where you treated him as an anticommunist. It's a fact that he was not a communist, but the people that were in his brigade, 6.000 people were killed, and families, homes were burned down only for the sake because they were not communists and that they were Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to enter into polemics about history, but I will stick to what is relevant for this case. So I don't agree with you, but I'll go on with my questions--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I interrupt again because matters are getting worse. You, Mr. Djordjevic, are making political statements to the witness; and the witness is answering them not only politically but personally. You are speaking of the counsel as though he was an enemy or an opposing force. This is a court. We are to decide guilt or innocence, not you. You should not address counsel as though he was an enemy. He has an important function to perform, a function that is responsible for the protection of a human right. We have to try and ensure that our proceedings are fair. Now, you should respect counsel and respect this Court, and we then in turn will respect you and your interests and respect the accused's and his interests and attempt to come to a just and fair decision. So if you would please, in future, show respect for the Court and counsel. And we would ask you, Mr. Djordjevic, to move away from a political debate and come to the facts of this case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just wanted to tell you that I wanted to ask the witness whether he was conscious of the fact that the territory of Kosovo and Metohija was in fact Serbian territory. That's constitutional, legal category; and I apologise if you misunderstood me, but my intention was nothing else than that. But I'll proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to you, Your Honours, I apologise. I said your state, your government, Yugoslavia. I have respect for the counsel. Maybe that was a misunderstanding. I didn't mean to show disrespect for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Hopefully from this point on, both counsel and the witness will behave in a more responsible fashion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The massacre of the 8th [as interpreted] of May, as you call it, you say you were one of the witnesses in the column; am I right? Saying that?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, what uniforms did you see members of, as you call them, the Serb forces wearing? Answer me that question: What sorts of uniforms did you see?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Are you asking me about the 2nd or the 3rd of May, because the 2nd of May what happened happened at night and I, frankly speaking, I couldn't identify the uniforms even though I tried hard, but it was dark, it was night, and it was very difficult to identify the uniforms. Maybe I have to thank the fact that it was night because otherwise they would have recognised me, and I wouldn't be hear to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you that because you said the police forces and then you mention that again, so that's what I'm asking you: What did you actually see?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, it's understood that they were forces belonging to the police and the army because it was -- the army forces had entered Bajgore mountains and used missiles and shelling, and the part that -- from -- through which the convoy was passing, there were paramilitaries, militaries, police, and forces. They were wearing masks, as I said, that's true; but when we came to the highway to Prishtina, a convoy of several APCs and other armoured cars passed by. So it was -- there were combined forces. First the police entered the population ranks, killed and did what they did, and the army supported the police actions by shelling. Counsel, this was done in a coordinated, in a concerted manner, by a commanding centre. It is not difficult to understand who they were. They were not extraterrestrials, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm certain of that too. But before it got dark, you say the army, the police, the paramilitaries, et cetera. So you saw members of these units, but -- all right. Explain what happened during the day before it grew dark and before all these terrible things happened, as you say, what kind of uniforms did you see round about? What kind of uniforms were worn by these people? You explain masks and so on, so explain that to us, please. To the best of your recollections, of course.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: You mean a day after when we were held hostages in a way in this co-operative, in this agricultural co-operative, or are you asking me about a period before that? I'm not clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I understood it that you described to us that the army and the police when the column set out and that was daylight, wasn't it? So what kind of uniforms did you see on that occasion? That's what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Usually the police -- the Serb army and police -- the police wore two kinds of uniforms, sometimes camouflage blue and there was another police force that they were wearing green camouflage with flak jackets, both of them. Sometimes they had with them people who were not wearing some special -- specific uniform, they were wearing only some ribbons, some headbands. It was, as I said, a combined force with paramilitaries, militaries --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there. You said "sometimes," but I'm asking you about the day immediately prior to the events that took place, not in general terms, but the day before, one day before the events occurred. Not when you say "sometimes" and things like that, but that very day.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's why I asked you to clarify your question because I was not clear. Look here, one day before the 2nd of May I didn't see any forces. I simply saw the shells falling over Sllakovc. They were throwing them in an uninterrupted way. I didn't see the police forces one day before that, as you are asking me. We saw the police forces in the dark, as I said, like silhouettes. But one day earlier we simply saw and heard the mortar fire and we left before the forces came, be them police or army forces. We simply fled, because if they saw me and if I saw him or them, they would have killed me. So we made sure to flee before they came. It was not a British army. They were fighting with the police.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: With the civilians. Correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said in your statement that you recognise some of the policemen. Can you clarify that, please?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if we could have -- I wonder if we could have a reference to the specific passage that my learned colleague is referring to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I tried to move quickly and I suggest that the witness tries to answer without me wasting time finding the reference, but he did indeed say that he recognised some of the policemen. I can find it, but of course I need a bit of time to do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 3rd of May, on the next day I was saying. That's true. You have it in my statement, but it's about the 3rd of May not on the 2nd of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And that's what I'm asking you about. The people you recognised, those policemen that you say you recognised, were they from Vucitrn?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This is on the 3rd of May?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So that we both understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, on the 3rd of May. Because the way you posed the question made me believe you are asking me about the 2nd of May, your counsel, that's why I was not clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, on the 3rd of May you recognised some police, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. I recognised many of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You want names, Mr. Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. But as he says he recognised them, I'm just asking him whether they were policemen from Vucitrn, the place he lived in; nothing more than that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: May I hear your answer?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Some of them, I knew that they were from the district of Vushtrri with the exception of Simic, who was from Decan district.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So these people that you recognised, that's what I'm asking you about.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This man too from the area, the district. Now, my next question is whether on the night of the 2nd of May you happened to recognise any policemen?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: No. They were wearing masks and it was dark, it was darkness. Frankly speaking, no. I tried to see if I could find some -- could recognise someone. May I explain something? The convoy consisted of 30, 40.000 persons. When the convoy was -- broke up after the shelling, this second part of the convoy, this was where these people were killed. Fortunately, I happened to be in the first part of the convoy. And the families that lost their members, some of them were entirely killed, they recognised some policemen and some policemen were from Gojbulja village, a village inhabited by Serb population. So the number of the killed was over 100. It was, as I said, a real massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would need 15 to 20 minutes more for my cross-examination; however, because of what is to follow, I suggest that we take a break now, the technical break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Our procedure technically requires that we allow time for tapes to be rewound, which is half an hour. We would normally have had our break in five minutes, but we will have it now and resume then in half an hour from now, at five minutes to 11.00, and questioning will continue for a short time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next question for you is this: Did you personally have any ties with the KLA; and if yes, what kind?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Personally, I didn't have any ties with the KLA. A brother of mine, who studied in Tirana, as it was impossible for him to come back to Kosova, he was wanted by the Serb authorities. From 1992 until the end of the war he remained in Tirana and dealt with logistical issues. He recruited members for the KLA, mainly Albanians who came from abroad to join the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me who Musa Terbunja is?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Musa Terbunja is an engineer in technology. We used to work together in the same school. When the war broke out, when Serb forces entered the villages, he went to the mountains and joined the KLA. He was a KLA member.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: He was a KLA commander? That's what you say in your statement.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: He was a local commander I would say, a platoon commander or something like that. I don't know what their organisation structure was, but, he was a sort of local commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: At page 12 of your statement, that's the last paragraph where you mention him, you say, among other things, that the bus driver told the Albanians who had gathered at the graveyard that the people would be taken to Macedonia, and you say that you went to Sudimlja, where you spent the night in the house of your friend, I asked you about him a little while ago. And then you say you went to Cecelija where the KLA had some sort of a headquarters. So what was the reason why you first went to the local commander and then to the Main Staff in Cecelija or whatever it was that the KLA had there?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: On the 2nd of May, I left the town illegally. There was no other way. I had to live in hiding, go to the mountains, or find a place to take shelter. I could not walk openly. So on the 2nd of May I went to Studime e Poshteme -- excuse me, it wasn't on the 2nd of May, it was earlier. I think it was a month earlier, 2nd of April if I'm not mistaken. So that night I went to Musa Terbunja's house to look for food. It was night when I left to go there. When I arrived in his house, I saw that there were many refugees staying there. Are you following me, counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: There were many refugees there, so I decided, since there was no room to spend the night there, there were many refugees, I decided to go either to the house of Musa's relatives. So to this day it's not clear to me whether I spent the night in Studime with his relatives or in Ceceli, not in the KLA headquarters but in the house of Fadil Beqiri, and that's where I stayed for a whole month. There were refugees there too, but I did stay there a month until the 2nd of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question is this: During the time that preceded the events in 1998 and 1999, as a citizen of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia were you criminally prosecuted or tried?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes. To my recollection, eight times we were taken, usually for interrogation at the police station and then before --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... were criminally prosecuted eight times?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: For offences. Do you want to know why?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: No. I'm asking you whether you were criminally prosecuted, not for a misdemeanour.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: In 1999, yes. I apologise. Before 1998, if you divide this period into two, so 1998 and post-1998. Before, I appeared eight times just because I taught students in Xerxe as a professor and as an activist of human rights. I spent 20 days in prison just because I was a professor, taught our students and pupils in houses, private houses, not in normal schools because we were expelled from schools in 1990. The police usually would come to the houses, arrest us there, maltreat us in the presence of our students, take us to police stations for interrogations, and then before court.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We have this in your statement, so I didn't want that. What I'm interested in is the criminal prosecution, when and why were you criminally prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I was criminally prosecuted once when I was arrested on the night of the 2nd of May between the two Studimes. So this is a different question. That's why I wanted to clarify. This is the only time I was criminally prosecuted. I was accused of being a terrorist despite the fact that I was among 30.000 to 40.000 civilians in the convoy. I was charged with terrorism, dear counsel, although throughout my life I worked as an activist of human rights and I taught children in schools. Do you want me to explain to you how they prosecuted me? I was arrested between the two Studimes --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What -- for what offence were you criminally --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The speakers are kindly asked to speak one at a time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about the 2nd of May when we were arrested and they opened the Smrekonica prison or camp. This is where we were arrested, thousands of us, about 1.000 were arrested and taken to Smrekonica prison, where they charged us for terrorist activity. This was about 13 or 14 days after the 2nd of May and they gave us document --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... for what court and was a judgement handed down?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I don't know who they were. There were civilians. There was a secretary, a recording clerk, and it wasn't a judgement but it was a decision to charge us with terrorism. They gave us a paper which read: I Sabit Kadriu was arrested in Qyqavica which was absurd since I was taken from the convoy in Studime. And when I said to them, You didn't arrest me in Qyqavica, you arrested me in Studime, he said to me: Who is asking you --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... time is precious. So I can conclude that you were never criminally prosecuted and that you were never convicted by any Serb court; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I was charged, criminally charged. I was issued this paper and these papers were taken from us once we were released to Smrekonica prison. I think it was stated in this paper that we were charged with this crime pursuant to Article 133. It was a monstrous prosecution. We were prosecuted en masse, issued these documents, maltreated. Many people died because of this torture. But as I said, this document was taken from us once we were released from the prison. I don't know why they took this document from us, but they did. We were in a camp, counsel --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... can I conclude that there was no trial. You never received a judgement that you are actually convicted of some crimes that you were involved in; that's what I wanted to get. Now I would like to ask you at page 14 of your statement you say, We learned that Professor Bajram Mulaku, former head of the DSK, the Democratic League of Kosovo from Vucitrn, Muharrem Shabani, and a villager from Sllakovc made a white flag and that they were leading the convoy. Can you tell us, if you know, what those people wanted, and what happened to them, what their fate was. Very clearly and succinctly.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I don't know why they did that. I didn't know who was leading the convoy, who was at the head of the convoy, but later on I learned that to my recollection, Ibrahim Muliqi; Bajram Mulaku, a professor; and Muharrem Shabani, a former activist in the municipality before the 1989, they had placed a white cloth on a branch and were leading the convoy. At one point in time, the convoy stopped moving. It is true that I was somewhere in the middle of the convoy, and there nobody knew why the convoy stopped moving. Together with a friend of mine, Fadil Beqiri, we started walking past groups of people and arrived at the head of the convoy, although it was difficult to get there. So when we got to the head of the convoy, I saw these three persons that I mentioned and I said to them, Why did you stop? Why don't we continue to move? They replied -- one said to me ironically, Who dares to carry this flag and carry on, then he's free to do so. They said that at Rashice hill, where the police and military forces were positioned, from this position the place where the convoy was could be clearly seen. So this white flag or cloth was placed and visible to the forces. They thought that somebody from the police forces would come and make a way for the convoy to move. When we saw that nobody was coming there, we said to these three persons, You have taken up the function of leading this convoy. Why are you not moving? And they said that there was a curfew and that we could no longer continue with our journey. The convoy was being targeted from behind as well. We were blocked from two sides. It was a valley from the two hills. There was firing. Before us was the Rashice hill where the police forces and military forces were stationed, and from behind there were also forces that had burned Studime and that were following us. So these people thought that it was better to pass the night there --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you to stop here. I want to ask you to stop here and let me ask you briefly whether those three men told you that they had been stopped by the KLA or not. Are you aware of it or not?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: There was no KLA there at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: The Serb forces were there, sir, positioned at Rashice neighbourhood. They had been positioned there for months in a row until the war ended. The NATO aircraft wanted to target them, but I don't know if they managed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now have a brief series of questions, and then I will complete my cross-examination. Am I right when I say that you don't have any first-hand knowledge about the killing of people in Galica, so that you're not in fact an eye-witness?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: That's not correct. I wasn't there when they were executed, but I was there when we found the corpses. Some villagers informed me, and I went there where these 14 bodies were lying. Some of the bodies were in a group like here, and three/four bodies about 15 or 16 metres further. I would like to inform you, counsel, that three of the bodies --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... there any eye-witnesses to the killing?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: From 22nd of May until the 24th of May when Qyqavica mountains and the villages in that area were encircled, starting from the point of Mitrovica and up to Obiliq, in this area more than 100 people were killed during this one operation that was carried out between 22nd of May and 24th --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you for the sake of saving the time to stop here and I want you to give me a short answer because my questions are short. We're talking about the killing of people in the village of Galica. Were there any eye-witnesses there, not about any other places? So were there any eye-witnesses to the killing of the people in the village of Galica?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Many because there were many civilians in Qyqavica. I withdrew these 14 corpses and other corpses in Qyqavica together with other people. We took this -- these bodies from the road, even their families were not aware of their killing. I found even bodies of my students, students that I taught. That's why I appeal for Mr. Vlastimir Djordjevic to carry out a catharsis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is the matter I warned you about. Would you please desist from that sort of comment. I think the answer is the witness is aware of no eye-witnesses of Galica. You're moving on?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The witness said that there were many witnesses, yet in his statement in paragraph 3, page 8, he said that there were no eye-witnesses of this massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now, the village of Oslan, the municipality of Vucitrn --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The speakers have to speak one at a time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, counsel, I need to clarify here. Will you allow me to make a clarification, a small clarification, about the youths from Galica? I have a file, a case file, containing the names of eye-witnesses. I went there shortly after they were killed, but there is a file here as an exhibit with the names of eye-witnesses. Of course maybe they were not there on the site. Had they been there on the site, they would have been executed too. This was not an army fighting another army. This was an army that was fighting with civilians. From the time of the Genghis Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It is clear that there were no eye-witnesses. Please leave Genghis Khan aside. If you want to answer my questions, fine; if not, I will have to put a stop to my cross-examination and then we will proceed differently. In the village of Oslan in the municipality of Vucitrn, the events from September 1998, am I right when I say that you don't have any direct personal knowledge of those events?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I do have knowledge. More than 14, I think 16 people were killed if I'm not mistaken. Ten years have passed, counsel, so I might be wrong, but this should be the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The interpretation is incorrect. Perhaps the interpretation is incorrect. I'm not asking you about your research after the events, but your direct knowledge. By that I mean that you were not present when it happened, you were not an eye-witness, unlike that situation in the night between the 2nd and the 3rd of May when you were a direct eye-witness. My next question: Is it correct that you don't have any direct knowledge of the events in Zivode [phoen] and Bivolak in September 1998?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: You're asking me questions and not waiting for my reply. Please show some understanding. From 22nd of September until the 24th of September, this massacre occurred. More than 130 civilians were killed. I was moving around. I come from those villages. I would go to Galica, I was go to Oshlan. I didn't happen to be there at the time of the execution, but I did see the bodies. We collected the bodies. We buried the bodies, counsel. If I was there on the execution site and witnessed their execution, I would have been one of the victims and wouldn't be here today. I was there, part of that civilian population there. So I moved about. I would go here then there, wherever I could. I have told you that we took part in the burial and in the withdrawal of these corpses because after they carried out their operation, the Serb forces withdrew. Only when Sadako Ogata came there, otherwise they wouldn't have withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... already. You testified about all that. We know all that. You've testified about this already. And as His Honour Judge Parker explained to you, all this is already part of the record. I'm just trying to clear up some things, and after that I can only conclude that you were not there at the scene and all the other conclusions are superfluous. My next question is this: Did you know in this case the 14 people, the eight people, the 12 people, did you know them personally, the people who were killed in those incidents? So I mentioned the locations, Zivoljude [as interpreted], Bivolak, Galica, Pecici, Balince, and so on? Did you know those people who were killed personally?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, there was some that I personally knew; however, you're commenting my previous answer. You're telling me that I wasn't there, there was no need for me to give an answer, and then you're commenting on my answer the way suits you best. And I don't think this is fair, counsel. I think you should show some understanding and allow me to answer. I said that I wasn't there when the people were executed, but I went there shortly after. They were buried on the same day when they were executed. As to your question whether I knew some of the victims, as I already pointed out, in Galice I had some former students that had been killed, a man with his two sons, another man with his two sons. Families have been completely destroyed. There is no perspective for them. Their houses have been destroyed. They've been mentally destroyed. I also knew Enver Haliti, a professor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You were asked if you knew some of the people. Your answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And part of the problem earlier, Mr. Djordjevic, is that you're asking whether the witness has knowledge. He has a lot of knowledge. I think you meant to ask: Were you present? Did you see the killings? No need for debate. I'm pointing out the cause of the problem. Okay. So the way you frame your question is very important, and then the witness knows how to answer it. When you ask if he has knowledge, you do --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bad interpretation, bad interpretation. [In English] Bad interpretation actually because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: All right. There's no need to go on and continue with the debate. I'm pointing out the source of the problem --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- because it's wasting a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's precisely what I asked, whether he was directly present, whether he witnessed that -- well, I don't know whether he understood. Maybe it's not his fault. I just want to find out what is right, what he knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
