utterances.text: Of course you said you knew some, you didn't know some. Do you know for sure that none of those people who were involved in those incidents, who were killed in those incidents at the sites we mentioned, do you know for sure that none of them were members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I know that one of them in Oshlan was a KLA member. He was not an active KLA member. I'm speaking about one person in Oshlan, Mustaf Shyti is this person. He's on the list. Respectable counsel, we're not trying to deny here that some people were KLA or not. If they were, they were, and their considered martyrs. The KLA dealt with the KLA members, those that had been killed during the war and they had been proclaimed martyrs. There are 46 KLA - I'm giving you the figure - that were killed and who were from Vushtrri municipality. As I said, the Serb forces were not always fighting the guerilla units. They were fighting the mass of people. They had thousands of civilians to pick from. They killed civilians, and that's what I'm here to testify about, the killing of civilians, not about the killings of KLA members. The KLA has its own judiciary, their own commanders, advocates, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now, as a member, an honorary member of the organisation to which you belonged, that is to say the council for the protection of human rights, do you happen to know how many civilians in Kosovo were killed? And I'm not asking you about the number of ethnic Albanian civilians but the total number of civilians killed?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I'm not the Zeus's head to have all the data and all members -- civilians living in Kosova. But according to the records of ICRC and other organisations, about 15.000 people were killed in Kosova. Perhaps this is not an exact figure because there are still 1.874 persons reported missing, and I would like to reiterate my request to ask the accused to clarify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will be enough, Mr. Kadriu. That's the third time you've come to that topic. Is there anything further, Mr. Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The 22nd of May, the massacre as you call it. The figures and information you have is information that you've gained indirectly because you weren't there yourself; am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: In a way, directly because when the war ended we visited all the families of the missing persons and compiled the records. And not only once, but I visited this family every year because whole families have been wiped out, their male members have simply disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My question is whether, when you conducted the many interviews you made within the frameworks of the council for the human rights -- for human rights, on crimes against the Albanians you say, do you have any information about the uniforms that the members of the Serb forces wore on that particular day, the 22nd of May; and if you do have information about that, please tell us what you know, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, I do have information on this. Part of my family was in Vushtrri that day, and in the eastern part of Vushtrri the military forces penetrated, that's where my family members were. Whereas, from the western part -- in the western part of the town there were operations, combat operations, carried out by combined forces, by Frenki's units and other regular units wearing different sorts of uniforms, and they expelled the civilians from town and gathered them at the graveyard. I think there were about 20.000 people who were expelled and directed to the graveyards --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Just about the uniforms, if you can tell us about those, please.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I'm absolutely positive, because I spoke to families, were camouflage uniforms, blue camouflage uniforms, green camouflage uniforms with vests. Some had helmets, some didn't, whereas at the site of the graveyard Vucina Janicevic held a speech, Ljubisa Simic, and Dragan Petrovic too before the mass of people. They were the leadership. Everybody who was older than 18 years old from the civilians recognised them, with the exception of some women maybe who didn't have the opportunity to go out very often. So they separated the men and took them to Smrekonica prison, about 700 or 800 of them, whereas 74 persons were executed with the family of Sezai. And the bodies of these 74 persons were transferred to Batajnica in the shooting range of Serb special police forces. And that's where they were found.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now my next question, since you mentioned Batajnica: Are there any witnesses to the gathering up of these bodies and them being transported to Batajnica amongst the people who you talked to?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: People saw the bodies being loaded on trucks and they mention how they recognised a driver with a last name Popovic. He worked for Kosovo Trans company. After they were executed, they were loaded onto trucks and taken to Batajnica, and that's where they were found in 2002 when the exhumations were carried out by ICTY representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The people you talked to who were survivors of the 22nd of May, did they tell you that they had recognised some of the people who were the executors on that 22nd of May?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: They recognised the people who expelled them from their homes, some of them. They were local policemen, whereas at the site of the 22nd of May massacre it is true that they didn't recognise them because they were wearing Balaclavas and they were with APCs. So on that day they were wearing Balaclavas, on the day of the execution, and the operation lasted just for a very short time. It was completely -- completed in a short time. There are people who said that they didn't even dare to look at these forces, otherwise they would have been picked up by them, separated, and executed. And you can imagine how human beings feel in such circumstances. All they want is to survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that completes my cross-examination. I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djordjevic. Ms. Kravetz, do you re-examine?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, no questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, you'll be pleased to know that is the end of the questions for you. As I've pointed out earlier, what you said today is merely in addition to your statement and the transcript of your previous evidence. So we have a great deal of information from you for which we thank you. We thank you for coming yet again to The Hague and the assistance you've been able to give, and you are now of course free to return to your ordinary life.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I did my best to be of an assistance to you; however, I don't think we can ever manage to cover all the cases. Things have developed in these ten years. There are many cases that I worked on and that have been not included in the indictment, for example, the execution of Selatin's family. So I leave this courtroom with this burden of not being able to mention each and every case despite my best efforts. Every time the time was limited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We appreciate that and you leave us with the burden of trying to properly determine the evidence in these matters. Thank you very much. The court officer will assist you out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner, your next witness is ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I hope he is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: While we -- the next witness is coming, I would just remind counsel of the programme next week because there have been a number of changes as we are accommodating other trials in the courtrooms available. We sit in the morning on Monday and in the afternoon on Tuesday and in the morning on Wednesday and Thursday of next week. And of course, Friday is a holiday and commences the break that we have already indicated until Tuesday, the 21st, when we resume. So morning Monday, afternoon Tuesday, morning Wednesday and Thursday. And we trust by then we have dealt with the witnesses that are planned for next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Mr. Neuner has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: What is your name and date of birth?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: My name is Dusan Dunjic. My father's name was Jovan, and I was born on the 8th of April, 1950, in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And in 2001 where did you work?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: In 2001 I worked in the Institute for Forensic Medicine in Belgrade, and I was the head of that institute at the time. And I started my professional career in the institute, and I am still a member of the institute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm referring here to your decision of the 11th of February, 2009, on the Prosecution's motion for admission of transcripts of evidence of forensic witnesses in lieu of viva voce testimony pursuant to Rule 92 bis. And in paragraph 1 and 2 of this decision, Your Honours have ruled to admit this witness's statement and his testimony from the Milutinovic case subject to him being available for cross-examination. And for the record I'm referring here to 65 ter number 2389, which is this witness's statement given on the 9th till the 11th of May, 2006. Could I seek to tender this document into evidence, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00526, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And in the spirit of this decision I would also seek to tender this witness's transcript which has the 65 ter number 5086 into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It also will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00527, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And, Witness, I understand that before you came here today you had an extensive opportunity to review both your statement and your testimony, and you agree with the contents of both, do you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I will now read out a summary of what the statement and this testimony contain. Dusan Dunjic was head of the Institute for Forensic Medicine at the University of Belgrade, and he still is. Mr. Dunjic supervised forensic exhumation teams which examined bodies at several sites in Serbia in 2001, including at the SAJ firing range, Batajnica, outside Belgrade. His team exhumed bodies from Kosovo at the exhumation sites coded Batajnica 1 and 2. In grave Batajnica 1, at least 36 bodies were exhumed. In grave Batajnica 2, 269 bodies were found. The witness identified and authenticated copies of the reports produced for these graves. The witness also described the process by which bone and other tissue samples were collected from the bodies for DNA analysis and states that he transported, November 2001, a series of such samples to Dr. Alonso for analysis in Madrid in Spain. The witness's evidence establishes the death of hundreds of Kosovo Albanian victims buried in graves in Batajnica. This witness's evidence is relevant to paragraph 75(d) and 75(h) of the indictment and its schedules D and H. Your Honours, in order to proceed efficiently with the exhibits adopted by this witness during the Milutinovic case, I would propose to simply read out each of the 65 ter numbers of these exhibits so that the Registrar could assign exhibit numbers for this case, if that pleases Your Honour I will proceed that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you remind us of the number of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I have counted 47, Your Honours, but I stand to be corrected. It could be one or two more or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you have the complete list there?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I have the complete list there. I forwarded it to the Registrar via e-mail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Have you provided a copy to Mr. Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic has received the witness notification sheet, Your Honours, which contains a few more documents, six or seven more documents. I have even in person consulted with my learned colleague before we met today in the courtroom and raised the issue and the Prosecution's intention that we are going to seek to tender documents this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If I could then ask Mr. Djordjevic, is there an objection to any one of these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we responded by electronic post to my learned friend about the documents that we won't be challenging and objecting to. I don't have it in hard copy now, but all the rest is contentious because when it comes to photographs, for example, we don't have the source, who took the photographs and pursuant to whose instructions. So we have problems with the photographs and we have certain findings which we cannot say we won't be objecting to. But we've informed the Prosecution about this. We sent our response electronically, so we're saying what we're not objecting to and what remains to be discussed during the proceedings today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm trying to be economical of time, gentlemen. The Chamber would be prepared to receive en masse but with separate numbers those exhibits to which there is no objection. And if there is, then, a second group of documents which are photographs as to which the issue is who took them, we can deal with that group of documents as one separate matter. What I'm not then clear is how many other documents we would be left with in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, in terms of the photographs, I've carefully listened to the suggestions from my learned colleague and I'm prepared to put some -- to lay a foundation to ask this witness who took photos so that we can then in a batch, meaning one by one, tender these photographs. There are then some 16 reports left according to my list. And if my learned colleague so wishes, I would be prepared to quickly ask this witness a few questions. The bottom line as far as the Prosecution understands it is that this witness has signed most of these reports himself, so I could walk the witness one by one through the documents. I'm not sure that so spontaneously I could condense everything. There are a few court orders which we believe are very reliable on its face, court orders to the effect that this witness and his team are to embark on performing such an exhumation in Batajnica. We would also believe that these are issues which can be dealt with quickly, Your Honours. And maybe even on cross-examination so that Your Honours can simply assign the appropriate weight to these documents after Your Honours have admitted them and my learned colleague had a chance to cross-examine this witness on these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, with respect to the reports, is your dispute with the authenticity of the report or is it with the correctness of the opinions expressed in the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Djordjevic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm not going to challenge the opinions of Dr. Dunjic, but we have a practical problem here, for example, the report on the abductions compiled by a team of seven or eight experts, pathologists, pathophysiologists and so on and so forth, and they signed the findings of the autopsy of one body. Now, what we have here, we have the findings of Lirija Beqiri [as interpreted], for example, the protocol of this; whereas we don't have a link with the DNA profile, which the witness here compiled. So that is why I cannot accept something that is Ba-12 without this link with the DNA analysis showing that it was based on the remains of Berisha Lirija [as interpreted]. So these are all matters that we could do is compare the findings of the OMPF where the head of that department was Jose-Pablo Baraybar, a witness we heard in court. However, for the time being I'm going to leave that whole issue for cross-examination or perhaps my colleague, Mr. Neuner, can deal with it in chief. Because from those findings and that protocol we don't really know who the person is, there's no identity, and with these -- and these seven pathologists say that because the body was decomposed, it was impossible to establish the cause of death, the identity of the person, and things like that. So those are the objections that I have to raise and we sent them yesterday afternoon to Mr. Neuner. Thank you. And there are a number of such protocols.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can we then try and break this up and move forward, Mr. Neuner. First, do you have the -- listed those proposed exhibits to which there is no objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I have. These are seven items which were listed in e-mail correspondence, and I'm prepared to read the 65 ter numbers out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What I'm thinking is that we will simply order that we receive the seven. You can provide the list to the court officer, and he will over the next break or at a convenient time following that, give them appropriate exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm in Your Honours' hands. I will proceed as suggested. So I skip, then, the seven agreed-to documents and move on to pictures or photos. And we are talking here about 26 pictures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, you wish to ask the witness a few questions about the photographs, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Witness, first of all, I understood from your evidence, your transcript, that the exhumations started in June 2001, did they?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, on occasion of these exhumations, why are pictures being taken?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Photographs are taken to document the job that is being done as evidence and as auxiliary resource for the identification, to facilitate the identification, because details of injuries are recorded as are details of the items and clothes that are found. So as part of the exhumation process and the autopsy that follows, all the details that might shed some light on the mechanism of injury, the kind of injury, the way in which injuries were inflicted, clothes, and so on are photographed. So elements that are needed for -- to identify the victim and also to determine the cause of death. As far as photographs themselves are concerned, photographs were taken at the time - and this is how it's done, it's done by the forensic technicians from the Serbian MUP on the orders of the investigative judge who issued an order for the exhumation and autopsies to be performed. And whoever is in charge of the exhumation and the autopsy in the field - and in this case that was me in Batajnica 1 and 2 - then asks for some things to be photographed and verified in this manner. In addition to the written document done by the medical doctor or anthropologist, a photo file is done. This is how we do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can you just, if you remember of course, tell us who was over the forensic technicians who took photographs in the summer of 2001? If you don't recall, just say so.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, believe me, I can't recall right now. I think it's in the report. I think that's in the report that I provided in June 2006. I think it was Petar, I don't know his last name, but he was a forensic technician who was assigned to us by the forensic department. It was done on the orders of the investigative judge Goran Cavlina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: With these explanations I'm just showing you a few pictures and then would seek Your Honours to tender them and a batch of these pictures.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If we could maybe look at 65 ter number 159 for a second, please. And I'm referring to page 1 here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yeah, in very brief terms, what is depicted here? Just in a sentence or two, please.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: This is the Batajnica 1 site. To the right you can see the tent. It is erected above the -- over the area where we carried out the exhumations. The tent on the left-hand side, as I'm now looking at the photograph, is the area where we did our expert analyses, examinations, and autopsies. The red vehicle is the -- a tank truck, and the white truck is in fact the refrigerator truck which is where we deposited the bodies that had already been examined by us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And who took this picture?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: The forensic technician.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If we can just move on for a second to page 2, please. -- I'm sorry -- we can tender -- these are a couple of pictures.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can you just say what this is here?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: We can see the entrance to the area where the exhumations were carried out, and there is the ground sheet, the tent above it, and this is the location of the exhumed area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And who took this picture?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: The forensic technician.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can I seek to tender this batch of photos, Your Honours, with the 65 ter number 159?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, do you maintain your objection to the photographs?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Although this is not usual procedure, I would like to ask the professor to tell me whether this is the forensic technician from the police or from the institute, the person that took the photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The evidence is that it's the forensic technician from the MUP, the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that the photographs were taken on the orders of the investigative judge. Did Professor Dunjic issue any orders? That's all I want to know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The investigative judge is in charge of the proceedings, and he appointed the forensic team. I was a representative. And from the Serbian MUP he obtained the forensic technician because we demanded that the forensic technician should be present there and he was and he took all the photographs of the course of our work and the autopsy. And we directed him, our --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will be sufficient. I do not object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djordjevic. The Chamber then has so far received seven agreed exhibits, which come under a category of capital A, and it now receives under category B of the schedule, prepared by the Prosecution, some 26 photographs. And the court officer will in due course allocate numbers, and they will be reported on. Now, the Chamber has briefly discussed what to do with the reports that are listed by the Prosecution for tendering, and what the Chamber proposes to do in respect of each of those reports is to receive them as an exhibit subject to the cross-examination that will be, where necessary, pursued by Mr. Djordjevic. So in a sense a conditional receipt at the moment; and if there is any concern at the end of the evidence, we will give further consideration to the question of the status of the exhibit. And those reports, therefore, are received. And that then leaves five further documents under category D. Do you feel that assistance would be achieved with respect of any questions to the witness about any of those?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: First of all, Your Honours, I wanted to note that four of these documents have been discussed already during the Milutinovic case. And in the schedule which I handed out to the Registrar, I have listed the transcript pages of the Milutinovic transcript where these four of the five documents had been already discussed. So we believe this in itself provides already some background explanation. The information was also put in our 92 bis motion on forensic experts, so they have thereby -- it has thereby been communicated to the Defence who could take this information on board to prepare its cross-examination today. Therefore, we would think that, yeah, on four of these documents we don't need to ask any further questions. I'm prepared to ask on the final document, 2411 is the 65 ter number, a few questions, and otherwise seek to tender all five documents, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter number 2411 on the screen for a second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Witness, if you just have a short look at this. That's just the first page. Can you explain -- or have you seen that document, first of all?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can you give a brief explanation about it.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: This is a list of documents that I forwarded to the investigative judge Milan Dilparic. Lest there should be any confusion, Batajnica 1 was managed by investigative judge Goran Cavlina; Batajnica 2 was managed by the investigative judge Milan Dilparic, that's why you have two last names being mentioned. This pertains to site 2. This is a list of documents that we submitted including the autopsy reports or protocols, the photographs, the exhumation protocols with the photo files, the anthropologist reports, the record of bones of individuals, list of loose clothes and items, and the list of items turned over to the court depository. This is the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You have given a very lengthy explanation about the document --

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: With which I would ask Your Honours to also tender this document with the 65 ter number 2411 into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the view that it will receive the five documents in the category D on the list, again subject to cross-examination, if any, in respect to each of these documents. So for the moment they will each be exhibits, and at an appropriate time the Registrar will indicate the numbers and you can proceed then on the basis that they are before the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I would have just one final small topic to deal with, and this is to facilitate the access to these pictures and to the documents by Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Witness, on some of the pictures, especially when bodies are mentioned, there are some codes -- signs with codes Ba dash and then a number follows. Could you just explain to Your Honours who assigned these codes?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Our team, my team. In accordance with an agreement gave the designation, Ba is the letter designation for Batajnica. And as far as the numerical designation is concerned, it is assigned to each body or body part identified on the site. And this number, it then goes together with this person and all the items associated with this person from the beginning to the end of the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Just one more question. If you told us you dealt with two mass graves Batajnica 1 and Batajnica 2. If you would or your team would assign a number for the first grave, how would that number look? Or a second question: If your team would assign a number for a body in the second grave, how in opposition to that, would this number look like?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: The second site would have number 2 in front of the letters Ba. That is the second location at Batajnica, and then the numerical designation for each body.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So if I have a body Ba-2 dash and then another number, from which grave would that be?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: That's from Batajnica 2. It either says Ba-2 or 2-Ba. Later on we adopted the approach to write 2-Ba, and that also pertains to Batajnica 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And if I would have a number Ba dash and then a number, from which grave would that be, Batajnica?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Batajnica 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. And in the interests of time and certainty, we would ask the court officer to file a memorandum listing all those exhibit numbers. Now, Mr. Djordjevic, your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Let me just get ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, you are a doctor of medical sciences. I would like you to just tell us briefly what area did you receive -- where did you receive your doctoral degree?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Forensic medicine.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question: I would now like to ask you to tell us briefly about your professional career from the time when you graduated, your specialisation, and your master's degree, all the way up to your doctoral degree. You are a witness here but you're also an expert.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, since I'm a witness, the colour of my hair tells you all you need to know about my career. So in 1976 I received my master's degree, M.Sc., and I received my doctoral degree in 1980. Both of these degrees are in forensic medicine. I, of course, have a degree in medicine. So in 1980 I received a doctoral degree in forensic medicine, and from my first job I have been working in the field of forensic medicine. I have published nine books, over 180 papers in professional journals. I testified in a number of cases throughout Yugoslavia and Serbia. And I was also -- I have also been asked to testify both for Defence teams before this Tribunal and for the Prosecution as an expert witness. I have enough professional experience because since 1990 I have worked a lot in the field, in Croatia, in Bosnia. I did research on torture victims of all ethnic backgrounds, not only Serbs, I would like to stress that, and several books were written about that. I dealt with the Racak case, the village of Racak. I also dealt with the Radonjic lake near Glodjane. It was a widely publicised case in Kosovo. And as for the other major cases, unfortunately I also did the expert report on the assassination of Prime Minister Djindjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next question, professor, is: Are you a permanently appointed court witness?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us since when have you been a permanently appointed court expert?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I think it's officially since 1980.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you explain to us what is it, the forensic medicine committee or board of the medical school in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: It is a body of the medical school in Belgrade which is considered to be the third-instance body for super-expertise. There are professors from various specialised fields and the court refers to it when the expert witnesses differ in their opinion about the same matter. And it's opinion, the opinion of the forensic medicine board - and there is also the forensic psychiatry board which is part of it - is the definitive opinion, the definitive report, which is then presented to the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The findings in Batajnica, Mr. Dunjic, were done by the commission of experts of medical doctors and you headed this commission?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The other members are Dr. Slobodan Savic, Marija Djuric, Dragan Jecenica, Vesna Djokic, Djordje Alempijevic, and Tatjana Atanasijevic. Now who put together this commission, was it you or was it somebody else's decision?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: It was my decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What was the decision based on?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: As the head of the institute, when I received an order from the investigative judge Goran Cavlina to set up a team to do the exhumations, with regard to the scope of work that could be anticipated I put together this team. But I had to leave some of my colleagues behind in the institute so that they could deal with the routine jobs of the institute. So I put together this commission from the personnel who could actually do that at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question: Professor, could you please explain to us the role of the forensic anthropologists on your team.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: The forensic role of the anthropologists in my team and in all teams of this kind, the role of forensic anthropologists is to assist us with the identification of the -- any injuries that could be found on the bodies, any changes to the bodies, and also to assist us to determine the sex, the age, the height of the body. It's an estimate that they do on the basis of the standards that the anthropology has at its disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any foreign observers who participated in your work or perhaps representatives of this Tribunal, the OTP; and if yes, who were they and what was their role? And do you have any particular observations that you would like to share with us in this regard?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: When Batajnica 1 was opened up, that was the first site, that's why it was designated with number 1, we were not aware of all the others. On the orders of the court, Goran Cavlina, and the president of the district court, Ms. Vida Petrovic-Kero, it was decided that only they could allow other persons to be present at the site itself. And all those who came first had to report to them to receive approval and authorisation; and once they were at the site, I gave my approval. But I strictly prohibited any interference with the professional work in the field. I prohibited any photography. So there is only one set of photographs, the photographs that we appended to our findings. Whatever else exists was not done with my approval or the approval of the court. We wanted to be as professional as possible, and at that time we received visits from a number of delegations. And Mr. William Fulton was there on behalf of the Tribunal and Brenda Kennedy, I believe, as an anthropologist, but they were there as observers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, what was Mr. Fulton's profession?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: As far as I can understand, he was an investigator because when we started doing our job we were able to obtain all kinds of equipment through him that we could not have obtained otherwise and that enabled us to do the job, gloves, overalls. We had a certain quantity of those items, but we went through them very fast. So we asked him to assist us and to get the overalls, the boots, and the gloves and all other supplies of this sort as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I assume that this answer that I'm receiving from you, that it has to do with Batajnica 1?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Both Batajnica "jedan" and Batajnica 2, it was the same principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well then. The same persons were present as far as the observers are concerned?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, I have to tell you that I don't really know. There was an NGO there too as far as I can recall or a human rights committee or something like that, I don't know what it was called. And there were two or three girls who took this in shifts, and they observed our work. But the daily reports were submitted only by me and only to the investigative judge who had issued the order. So all of their reports and so on are not official. The only official thing is the report that I submitted to the judge orally and in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The Defence is particularly interested in knowing whether the exhumation -- exhumations were ever attended by the representatives of the OPMF [sic]. I don't know if you know who they are, what that is.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please translate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I thought so. It is an UNMIK body that deals with forensic medicine in Kosovo and pathology in Kosovo, and it was headed by Mr. Jose-Pablo Baraybar, an anthropologist.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: The first time that I met Jose-Pablo Baraybar was in the Forensic Medicine Institute. He came there as part of the UNMIK team, and since, at the time, I was in charge of all the things that were being done at Batajnica and at the same time I was a member of the coordination centre of the Serbian government for Kosovo and Metohija, after the first exhumations at Batajnica 1 followed by Batajnica 2, there was a problem of how to identify the bodies. And we took bone samples, we stored those samples, and I personally took the first batch of those bone samples on the orders of the court to Madrid. The DNA profiles from Madrid that we got back, we had to compare them to the data collected by UNMIK because we didn't go to Kosovo. UNMIK collected blood samples from the relatives of the missing persons and took post mortem information for the purpose of identification, stories from other people. And we used those elements to identify the victims, and on the orders of our court and our judge, Judge Dilparic, a comparison was made. And this is the first time that I met Mr. Baraybar who came there. And an arrangement was made that all those who had gone through our identification process and who had been exhumed at Batajnica 1 and 2 sites should be transferred back to Kosovo once their identity had been determined. And that was the first time that I learned that all these bodies that we transferred to Kosovo through the coordination centre were then examined by some persons. I didn't know who those persons were. So the bodies that we exhumed and examined and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now, professor, you said that you carried certain parts of the skeleton for DNA analysis to Madrid; did I understand you correctly, that you took them to Madrid, and I assume that they were parts of bones, ribs?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: No, they were samples of the femur, 2 centimetres of femur were taken. And if an arm was found, for example, separate from a body and anthropologically it couldn't be incorporated into the remains of a body found somewhere else, then we would take a sample of the upper arm bone, the shoulder bone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Was that enough to establish DNA profiles and to identify the individual concerned?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: It was sufficient only for establishing a DNA profile. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Is that what UNMIK did?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: For the DNA profile to be able to be compared with something, then a DNA profile of the blood had to be taken of persons reported missing. And then by correlating those results and comparing them, you can establish who the person was and whether it's the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: As we're coming up for our technical break now, I have one more question before we do break to round off this topic and it is this. What I'm interested in now is the following: Did you take from all the bodies in Batajnica 1 and 2 samples of the femur or arm bone or whatever in order to establish the DNA profile as you said, and did you take them to Madrid?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Only from Batajnica 1, we took samples only from Batajnica 1 to Madrid as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now, what happened to the remains from Batajnica 2 relevant to DNA profiles?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: All the samples that were taken, we then consulted the judge and reached an agreement with him and he contacted the ICMP, whereby they should take over the samples, because at that time, the end of 2001/2002, a DNA laboratory had already been established in Sarajevo I believe. And after that we, in our institute, got a DNA laboratory and there was another one in Banja Luka. So these three independent institutions analysed the DNA profiles obtained. And as far as Batajnica 1 is concerned, the samples from Batajnica 1, and the bone samples from Glodjane or the Radonjic Lake, which I did with my team, those samples were also taken to Madrid. So those two sets of samples from Glodjane or lake Radonjic, the victims found there in 1998, and the ones from Batajnica 1 dating to 2001. So it had to be done that way in order to gain permission and authorisation from the president of the district court and to keep it within the confines of the law for this biological material to be taken abroad for identification or other DNA analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I propose a break now, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We have our second break now, and we'll resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, you said that the first DNA laboratories in the Balkans started up when Sarajevo received its and then this was followed by Belgrade and Banja Luka; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say the Balkans, but in our former Yugoslavia. I think that in Zagreb a DNA laboratory began to work parallelly, and in our institute this was in 2002, the end of 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What I didn't understand very well was this: Batajnica 2, your commission, the team of experts, did you take from the bodies there, samples for obtaining DNA profiles or not, as was the case with Batajnica 1?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now I have an aide-memoire here, the 15th of September, 2001, samples were taken of bones from the -- of samples from the femur, not one sample but two samples, and these were taken from the Batajnica 2 location.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And did you obtain the DNA profiles for persons from which you took the samples for the DNA analysis?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: The ICMP, which was a mediator, that is to say the International Organisation for Missing Persons, they sent us successively, as the groups were processed and identities established, they sent us these successively because they had the DNA bone samples that we sent to them pursuant to authorisation from the court and they had the DNA profile from the bloods -- the blood samples taken from family members who reported these persons missing and this was supplied to them by UNMIK from Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: When you obtained this material, the material you say you received from that institution, did you also receive the identities of the persons, wherever that identification was made possible?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, that's a complicated question. It's complicated for me to answer it, but it boils down to the following: The DNA profile that we received, and that's what the report looks like, you have the DNA profile of the bones with a marking that we found in the locality and they are numeric values. Then you have the DNA profile by name and surname obtained from the blood samples of one, two, or three relatives and that was sent in by UNMIK. And on the basis of all that together, the ICMP concluded that the person from which the blood sample was taken was named such and such. Now, that's not where the identification process ends. It doesn't end there because, based on our experience and in cooperation with our experts for genetics or expert for genetics, we now performed a comparative analysis. And the post mortem information in written form taken by UNMIK about the missing persons, for each individual person, was compared. So when I got to know Jose-Pablo Baraybar, that data was written down and compared to our autopsy and anthropological findings and also with the DNA protocols and reports that came in to us from the ICMP. And then we correlated them all, compared and contrasted the data to see whether it all corresponded and whether it was the person in question. And then as a team, as a commission, on the basis of all the parameters available, we would make our conclusions that in such and such a case Batajnica 1 or Batajnica 2 it was such and such a person on the basis of all the analysis that went beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That makes things much clearer. What I'd like to ask you now is this: When we speak about your work on Batajnica 1 and 2 and your meeting -- meetings with Jose-Pablo Baraybar - you said that he came to visit your institute - so in relation to those two events, that is to say the exhumation process of Batajnica 1 and 2, when did he actually appear? What point in time did he appear?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, I really can't be precise. I'm trying to think back and remember, but I think it was already once we had completed the analysis of Batajnica 2 and when the first DNA analyses coming back to us -- coming in to us and when the first repatriations began. And you're asking me when that was? Well, I can't be precise. I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to your involvement in the exhumation process and the expert analyses and so on and so forth and as you headed the team of experts, did you know whether there was a protocol on cooperation between UNMIK or the OPMF - which is how UNMIK functioned, the forensic medicine and pathology institute that Baraybar headed - and the Serb authorities? Was there a protocol on cooperation of any kind between these instances?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, please believe me when I say I don't know anything about that. I just happened to hear or there was some information going round as a piece of information that they asked for something like that and sought to obtain something like that, but I personally don't know about that because it was the time when on both sides of the border there were requests and demands for identification and for uncovering the missing persons, the ones from Batajnica and in Kosovo itself because our experts couldn't go there. I couldn't go to Kosovo with my team nor could other experts from our country. They couldn't go there to look for remains or conduct exhumations for persons that were known to have gone missing in Kosovo. And the only time I was there was in 1998 and in January 1999 when I did Glodjane and Racak. After that, after the bombing, in 1999 that was impossible. I couldn't go there as an expert. And then there was this tension all the time as to whether a team from Serbia could go to Kosovo to do the exhumations or could an Albanian team come to Batajnica. And a colleague of mine, he was an Albanian from Pristina, I believe, I can't remember his name just now, he was a younger colleague of mine, came to see how we proceeded Batajnica 1 and 2. He would come to the institute. He said he was very pleased to come and see. We would say we were very pleased to have him because there was no question of concealing anything. So this was as far as professional information was concerned and the exchange of that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now, in all these unfortunate circumstances, mention is made of two more locations, they are Petrovo Selo and Perucac. There was another team working there headed by Dr. Radovan Karadzic. You know him?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, certainly. He is an assistant professor in Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Your colleague. And he headed one of those teams unless I'm very much mistaken?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: In Petrovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Now, linked to this protocol on cooperation you say that you have it -- have some very vague information about that and that you think you heard something about that, but anyway this agreement envisaged cooperation between the OPMF and the competent authorities dealing with the same things you were dealing in, that is to say the autopsy findings for Batajnica 1, 2, Petrovo Selo, Perucac, and so on. Now, as you just told me that you know Dr. Karadzic, do you happen to know that Dr. Radovan Karadzic ever, if you didn't, and I conclude that you didn't, did he ever have any contacts with anybody from the OPMF?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. I know this colleague of mine from meetings. I know my colleague Mr. Karadzic from professional meetings, he's a forensic specialist. Now, who he contacted with and whether he contacted with them, I really don't know. I have no idea. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now, would you have had to have known had there ever been a meeting along those lines you personally, would they have had to inform you about it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, let me put it like this. I have to turn my mind back to that period when we began the repatriation process for the exhumed remains and autopsy findings from Batajnica 1 and 2 because we had the question of storing the bodies that were -- we conducted autopsies on. Repatriation was carried out, and on one occasion there was a lady doctor, she introduced herself as being a forensic expert. Whether she was Kozlowski or some surname like that, and together with our assistants who were in this group she examined those bodies so as to see that in the bags marked with number such and such, Batajnica such and such, there was indeed a body, whether there was an autopsy protocol she looked to see what we had established. And then those bodies were placed in a truck, taken across the border, and repatriated. Now, what happened after that over there, I really don't know. Whether somebody examined those bodies over there, a younger colleague of mine told me that they were going to carry out another autopsy, whether they did or didn't or what they did, I really don't know. And I have no written trace of anybody doing anything to the bodies after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying, after listening to your answer just now, that you have absolutely no knowledge whatsoever about what the OPMF did with the repatriated bodily remains of the former citizens who were ethnic Albanians?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when you said that you received a report of some kind from a younger colleague of yours or was it a summary of the findings and examinations done by the OPMF?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: The colleague just informed me orally because he had taken part in the repatriation process. So actually, our commission that worked on Batajnica 1 and 2, I delegated him to keep in contact with this Dr. Kozlowski, the lady doctor, and he was accompanied by UNMIK and our organs that transported those bodies from the body to Kosovo. And then he told me orally - and this was six or seven years ago - he said to me, We've handed everything over, and we have the list of the bodies that we handed over. We couldn't hand over all the bodies at once nor were all the bodies identified. This went on successively over a period of two years. Anyway, he handed them over the list, and I think we also agreed with Judge Dilparic that we supplied the autopsy protocols in electronic form so that they could have both, the hard copy and the electronic information, and the bodily remains, and confirmation of death because when a doctor establishes death they write out a certificate, a death certificate. And he said that it appeared that they would be examining all of this. Whether he heard about it or saw it, I really don't know. That's all I know about that. This is the information he gave me orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know where he got the information from?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, probably in his contacts with those people over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I'll just briefly interrupt the cross-examination, and I'd like to put something right because my associates have drawn my attention to something that I misspoke, that I kept saying OPMF where it should be OMPF. OMPF is the acronym for the organisations. And now I'll continue and I would like to ask the usher to pull up P4554 [as interpreted], page 2 --, or rather, page 27, paragraph 2 of the B/C/S. [In English] Not page 27, second page, paragraph -- no, no, page 27, okay. [Interpretation] Yes, page 27, para 2. P4554 [as interpreted] and page 25 of the English. May we have that pulled up. We're still waiting for the B/C/S. That's not it. [In English] Page 27 in B/C/S. 25 in English -- this is not the right document definitely. The ERN number is K053-5916. Maybe it's better to say. It is appendix C and D of the witness statement of Jose-Pablo Baraybar, P454, that is the right document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Exhibit P454?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And page 27 in B/C/S and 25 in English. So it is in B/C/S -- B/C/S page 2, definitely, not 27 -- no. So it is 27. Now -- in e-court it's page 14 am I right and it should be page 2 in B/C/S, same document. This is page 14 here. Can we --

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Maybe my learned colleague has a hard copy and can work on the ELMO with hard copy --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I have one, I have one. It is -- it's not correct definitely. [Interpretation] Can I please ask the usher to take the -- this document in hard copy in B/C/S and to show it to the witness and then to place it on the ELMO. I, however, underlined, as I worked on the case, some elements, and I circled some elements; and now I would like the witness to read the elements that I circled out loud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The report consists ..." Is that what you want me to read?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The report consists of four parts. The first is an introduction to the analysis of human remains found in mass graves and the need to 'formulate' the most probable cause of death, Baraybar and Gasior 2006," that's the reference, "whenever possible. The second part explains the nature of forensic examinations while the third deals with the results of those examinations comparing the findings with the initial results provided by the Serbian organs. Finally, the fourth part contains the conclusions."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now my question in this regard --

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we are starting here in the middle of a report. I'm not intending to object at this point in time; but perhaps my learned colleague can lay a certain foundation, such as whether this witness has seen the report, is familiar with the report. We are jumping into the middle --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner, I believe we should allow Mr. Djordjevic to proceed. I anticipate he's going to ask for comments on this procedure as outlined there. And so we'll see whether it gets into the difficulties you are anticipating or not. I think it will stop short of those. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. My colleague Neuner will hear my next question and will see that there was no reason for concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that forensic anthropologists, by analysing the skeletons in addition to the parameters that pertain to the identity of the person in question - here I'm referring to the sex, age, and height - can also determine circumstances surrounding the cause of death by reconstructing the injury and trauma. Is this their job? Can they do that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Whether they can -- as to whether they can determine the cause of death, no, they cannot because they are not doctors. Anthropologists are not doctors. They are trained to those -- to do those things that you mentioned first, but it is only medical doctors. Forensic pathologists have the requisite expertise to be able to determine the cause of death, or rather, to provide the court with facts, and on the basis of which conclusions can be drawn as to the cause of death. So an anthropologist does not have the requisite expertise to talk about the cause of death without consulting a forensic medicine specialist. He can assist us by providing partial explanations that pertain to the skeleton, but not about the cause of death or the sequence of injuries or the time when injuries were inflicted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yeah, I just have to say that what was asked here of this witness was an opinion, and we have today a fact witness with us who can certainly express or is invited here to express his knowledge about what he observed and what he saw. But what Your Honours have just heard is an opinion about another witness and the work of another witness who has appeared here in this trial. And we still don't have a basis for why that witness should know about this, and I believe that this is not appropriate at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Neuner. We have heard fully the expertise and training of the witness, and at this moment the comment does not appear to have moved outside of his precise area of expertise as a forensic pathologist. Thank you. Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next question is this: What was the condition of the bodies at Batajnica 1 and 2? Is there a general description that could fit all of them or should we go body by body?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I will try to be as concise as possible. The general description, the general characteristic for Batajnica "jedan" and Batajnica "dva," Batajnica 1 and Batajnica 2, is that those bodies were in various stages of putrefaction, as we call it, in terms of soft and hard tissue. That would be the expert description. And we forensic medicine experts pay particular attention to this, to the changes in soft and hard tissue. I'm sorry I can't really see you because of the ELMO, so I have to crane my neck. So we pay attention to those changes to the soft and hard tissue in order to be able to determine whether any changes observed on the body were caused ante or post mortem, whether the changes were caused by injury, whether the injury was inflicted by a specific implement, and at the same time the post mortem injuries help us determine indirectly the time of death. That would be it in brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What I can draw as a conclusion from this is that the cause and manner of death, in all the cases where your commissions carried out the autopsies, were not determined because, you state this as a reason, bodies were in an advanced state of decomposition; am I right when I say this?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I have to continue. Since I'm here testifying as a witness who has expertise in forensic medicine, I feel this need to explain, to tell the Trial Chamber, that I have testified before as an expert and as a fact witness. I come from the Forensic Medicine Institute in Belgrade which is one of the oldest such institutes in south Europe, I'm not going to say the Balkans. And our forensic medicine practice is based on the best practice, German practice, with some additions from the Anglo-Saxon forensic medicine programme and elements from the Russian forensic medicine programme, so that we bring together the three strongest approaches in this field. And in the Forensic Medicine Institute in Belgrade, where I come from, there are textbooks and books that were published as early as 1850, written by our experts. And all the other institutes in the former Yugoslavia stem from our institute. So that's it as far as our approach is concerned, our school of thought. Everything that I'm saying, my evidence, is an -- the evidence of a professional, and this is how it's done throughout the world. Facts are one thing, they have to be processed in a certain way. And then on the basis of this fact conclusions are drawn, that's another element, and there is a third element, the interpretation of the facts or, in other words, provision of an opinion for this Tribunal. And for any court, national court or this one here, what is important is the consistency between the findings and conclusions on the cause of death. That means that if in the findings you do not have the elements that would enable you to claim for an injury, for instance, that it was caused while the was still alive, then in the conclusion you must not put that this injury caused the death of the individual. And that is why this concept is used, the body is in an advanced stage of degradation due to putrefaction and cause of death cannot be determined. What does it mean for practical purposes for a court? This means that the cause of death is the injury for which you, as an expert, have to prove that it was caused while the individual was still alive. Now it may sound slightly ludicrous to you now, but there are injuries that can be inflicted post mortem or immediately before death, and they can look the same. Because there is no soft tissue, and you cannot determine vital functions. You cannot determine when the injury was inflicted. And now, a through and through wound of the skull on a skeletonised body, one can assume that this injury caused the death of the individual. One can assume that. But as an expert, I have to answer to you or anyone else in court, what is evidence in proof of the fact that this caused the death? I look at the autopsy report, I see that the body was skeletonised, and I say, Look I'm sorry, I don't have proof. It is my opinion. Why is this important particularly when it comes to exhumed bodies? Not only in Batajnica. I testified as an expert for the Defence in Srebrenica cases and some other cases. Why is that important then? It is important because there are several different injuries that could be inflicted in various time-periods before and after death. And if you find three or five through-and-through wounds to the body, you cannot determine first of all the sequence of those injuries and you cannot determine whether they were inflicted while the individual was still alive because only the injuries that were caused while the individual was still alive could be taken as possible causes of death. So to make this very clear because I saw an image of a skull with a through-and-through wound, gun-shot wound, I can say this as a forensic medical doctor and an anthropologist cannot say that. A person has a through-and-through wound with the exit -- with the entry wound on the right temporal bone and the exit wound on left temporal bone. I examined one such person who was still alive. It was a soldier who had tried to commit suicide by firing a pistol into his head. He tried to sue for damages, and I had to examine him. He had a bone defect, you could determine that by looking at the X-rays. So if you look at this person -- so he was alive when I examined him. If he died and his body became skeletonised, what would the anthropologist conclude as to the cause of death? He would conclude that this person died because of this through-and-through wound to the head. That would not be true because he may have killed himself or died in some other way, and he lived for three years after this suicide attempt. I examined him three years after that. So when I testify in court, I stick to my specialty which is forensic medicine. I have to provide you with evidence, and I have to be consistent. Our conclusions, conclusions that cause of death could not be determined, are absolutely consistent with the findings that we put down. And the forensic medicine doctory [as interpreted], not only in Serbia but throughout the world, is based on this and all the rest is just assumptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next question for you, Doctor: What was the state of the -- what could have been the state of the remains when they were brought to Kosovo? As you know, it was the period -- well, the repatriation lasted from 2004 to 2006 at the time when the UNMIK commission carried out its examinations as I indicated a little while ago. So what could have been the condition of the mortal remains. When was it that you did it, in 2001?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So it was three, four, five years later?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Based on your experience?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, not only based on my experience but based on what I know. When we started the repatriation of the bodies that we had exhumed and autopsied, the decomposition on those bodies that we verified at that time were even more pronounced. What do I want to say? The moment you remove a body from the soil and expose it to air, in particular in summertime which was the case when we were doing the job, the putrefaction of soft tissues picks up pace so that most of the bodies that we had repatriated were almost fully skeletonised. So the degree of skeletonisation was much higher than at the time when we autopsied the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, on the basis of your findings when you deal with bodies that are as decomposed as the ones that we have here, taking into account the remaining soft tissue on the skeletons, in some cases you can determine the manner or the mechanism of injury and the cause of death of the person being autopsied?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't understand you all that well. Are you referring to the autopsy of people who died recently or the exhumed bodies?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The exhumed bodies.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, when you're dealing with exhumed bodies, bodies that have spent a longer or shorter period of time buried in the soil with putrefaction present to a greater or smaller degree, the injuries that can be identified in hard tissue, in the bones in other words, or on the remnants of soft tissue can assist in divining the mechanism of injury. But the thing that is very important for every injury, and let me go back to what I said before, is to determine the time when it was inflicted, in other words, whether it was inflicted ante mortem or, indeed, whether it caused the death of the individual, or whether it was post mortem because there are post mortem injuries that might appear or indeed appear just like injuries that are inflicted while the individual was still alive, in particular when we're talking about injuries caused by blunt objects, blunt trauma. The same goes for gun-shot wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since I know that there will be no trial this afternoon in this courtroom, I don't know whether you would allow me to go on and try to finish cross-examining this witness today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We can go on at the most till 2.00. Our problem then is that certain support staff are finished their time and must leave. So another ten minutes and that will leave five minutes for --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try. I'll do my best. If not, we'll have to continue on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next question: On the bodies exhumed at Batajnica, by that I mean Batajnica 1 and 2, were there any obvious military items, clothes, footwear?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't really remember that at Batajnica 1 there were not, as far as I can recall; on Batajnica 2 there were some items camouflage pants, for instance, or there was one case. I remember that at one point we found in the trousers wore by a male victim the string that is used to clean the barrel of a rifle. It has a piece of cloth on it and then you pull it through the rifle barrel to clean it. That's what we found, and I have to note that there were mostly males in Batajnica 2. I don't know the number of those persons. We didn't do this kind of analysis, but we did describe and photograph everything that we found.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Based on your experience and knowledge, in the bodies that have spent at least two months under water, can you determine the cause of death, for instance, drowning or anything else?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, now you've put me in a situation where I have to both answer you and not answer you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, give it a try.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, with your indulgence, Your Honours, I am a witness here. But I can tell you as an expert that a body that has spent a certain period of time under water, if the water is cold, that there was no animal attacks, that there was no major decomposition of the body, just of course there is a certain degree of putrefaction, even if the body's in the water that would also depend on the health condition of the person, the kind of injury. In our climate there is putrefaction, and it is very difficult to determine whether this person found in the water drowned because bodies that are found in water are not necessarily drownings, all of them, it doesn't necessarily mean that they drowned and that this was the cause of death. There can be various causes of death and bodies are then found in the water.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The same situation, a body that has spent at least two months in the water, can one make a distinction between a body and putrefaction fluid?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Between blood and putrefaction fluid.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Putrefaction fluid looks a lot like blood, and putrefaction fluid gathers in some areas of the body and it is a kind of dirty red colour, that's why it's called putrefaction fluid and not blood. But if the bodies in the water, the red blood cells are -- get washed away by the water, so you can no longer -- you can no longer determine the difference between the putrefaction fluid and blood because there is a smaller concentration of red blood cells in the putrefaction fluid. But if there was a substantial loss of blood, there will be less red blood cells in blood itself, so it is difficult to determine which is which. But there are various elements that contribute to this that have an effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Again, the same situation, a body is at least two months in the water and there are parts of clothing and there are stains on the clothing. Is it possible, by observing it, to determine whether this is blood or, for instance, putrefaction fluid or some -- something else?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, this is the situation where I had -- where I would have to analyse quite specifically as an expert in order to be able to give you a specific answer. It would depend on a number of factors, first of all, the kind of fabric, whether there was injury or not, injuries that might have bled. For instance, if you have an injury to the arm, there could be some stains on the leg, but at any rate it is an expert analysis. I'm still here as a fact witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you determine on human remains that have decomposed on a body, in other words, for instance the distance from which this person was killed if it was a gun-shot wound fired from a pistol or a rifle?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: If there is decomposition and if no spectrographic analyses are carried out on the entry wound, which has been identified, and if there is no analysis done in this manner, it is very difficult to determine solely on the basis of the appearance of the injury and the trajectory of the projectile the distance from which it was fired. Decomposition destroys a lot of trace evidence, for instance, gunpowder residue because gunpowder usually remains at the first barrier, for instance, clothes. But if the barrel was right next to the skin, then it will remain on the skin and will penetrate into the bone. But with decomposition a lot of this trace evidence gets lost because primarily the bodies are buried, there is humidity and/or even water and the trace evidence gets washed away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And is it possible solely on the basis of the appearance of the entry and exit wound on tissue that has been decomposed and on the wound channel or canal to determine the calibre of the round that caused the injury and what are the criteria?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: There are injuries -- well, if there are gun-shot wounds, you can have a gun-shot wound to the soft tissue and to the hard tissue. Once there is decomposition, there is no more soft tissue, we can only make analyses of hard tissue, of bones if there is any injury. There are bones such as the skull, the pelvis, and then there are long bones, the humerus, the femur, there are soft bones such as the facial bones and so on. And there are specific and peculiar injuries to those bones that make it possible for us to claim, with a high degree of certainty, that they were caused by a projectile. So now let me go back to your question. Only a round that hits the bone at a right angle can leave a relatively accurate calibre, the diameter. But let me now tell you what this looks like, let me draw an analogy. When a projectile leaves the muzzle of a fire-arm, because of the land and grooves it rotates along its longitudinal axis. But the rear end of the projectile also exhibits some kind of motion. When it hits the first barrier, and that's skin - or it can be indeed anything else - assuming that it's skin, it already changes its position because of the rotation. This is rotation at huge speed. It's a small mass travelling at a high speed. It causes a hole, a defect in the form of a hole, but you cannot get the exact calibre. We can make an approximation. We can say this is maybe about 7 millimetres, it's not 12 millimetres, so we can't be accurate, completely accurate. Once the projectile hits the barrier, once it moves through the bone, it changes its -- it doesn't change its trajectory. It moves in the same direction, but it tumbles, it rotates the round, the bullet, which is now inside the body. And then when it leaves the body, when it exits the body, perhaps only the bullet will leave and the casing may remain in the body. And this results in the exit wound being much larger than the entry wound on the bone, but this is provided that the bullet hit the bone at the right angle. It is the only situation in which we can determine the approximate calibre. It's not the kind of calibre that would be relevant for the Court -- you cannot really determine whether the calibre was 7.65 and not 7.62. We can only say in terms of our testimony before the court that this was a bullet fired from a weapon with a calibre of less than 10 millimetres. That would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately I have many questions for you, so I won't be able to complete it now. We'll have to continue on Monday. The reason is, of course, your grey hair and your huge experience, but unfortunately I'm forced to do that in order to be my job properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We appreciate the situation, Mr. Djordjevic. I'm afraid, Professor, we must ask if you can return on Monday. I think we can expect, though, that your continued cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: At least half-hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- half an hour. And that being so, your re-examination will then follow, Mr. Neuner, on Monday. Unfortunately we have run out of time. The court officer will give you some assistance as to your return on Monday, times and so forth, and in the meantime we must adjourn now, and we look forward to the completion of your evidence on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 6th day of April, 2009, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25
